notes.subtopic: 1. From the League of Nations to the UN

fiveW.who: Victors of World War I; later Roosevelt and Churchill
fiveW.where: Geneva (League); San Francisco conference; UN HQ New York
fiveW.why: To prevent world wars after WWI and WWII
fiveW.how: League failed in the 1930s; Atlantic Charter and San Francisco Conference created the UN

notes.content:
**League of Nations** — founded after the horrors of **World War I**; first session **1919**.
• **First international organisation** for peace and cooperation.
• Kept peace in its early years, but **failed in the 1930s** as the **Axis Powers (Germany, Italy, Japan)** grew powerful → **World War II (1939)**.

**United Nations** — planned from **1941**, during the war, to avoid future wars.
• The name **'United Nations'** was coined by US President **Franklin Roosevelt**.
• Keyword **Embargo:** economic/diplomatic sanctions against a hostile country.

notes.subtopic: 2. Atlantic Charter and Birth of the UN

fiveW.who: Winston Churchill (UK PM) and Franklin Roosevelt (US President); delegates of 50 nations
fiveW.where: On board a battleship; San Francisco
fiveW.why: To build lasting peace after the war
fiveW.how: Charter proposals, Declaration by United Nations (1942), San Francisco Conference (1945)

notes.content:
• **14 August 1941** — **Churchill and Roosevelt** signed the **Atlantic Charter** on a battleship; its proposals became the **basis of the UN**.
• **January 1942** — **26 countries** signed the **Declaration by United Nations**.
• **25 April 1945** — **San Francisco Conference**; **50 nations** drafted the **UN Charter**.
• **24 October 1945** — UN came into existence → **United Nations Day**.

**Facts**
• **51 original members**; now **193** (all in the General Assembly).
• **HQ: New York, USA**.
• **Six official languages:** English, French, Chinese, Russian, Arabic, Spanish.
• Funded by **member nations**.

From the **Preamble of the UN Charter**:
• Maintain **international peace and security**.
• Promote **human rights** everywhere.
• **Save future generations** from war.
• **Equal rights** for all persons.
• Promote **justice, freedom and social progress**.
• Respect for **international law and treaties**.

**Memory hook:** Peace · Rights · Future · Equality · Progress · Law.

fiveW.when: GA meets once a year; non-permanent SC members serve 2 years
fiveW.what: GA = world parliament; SC = keeper of peace
fiveW.why: To discuss world issues and take binding decisions on peace and security
fiveW.how: One nation one vote in the GA; veto power of the five permanent SC members

notes.content:
**General Assembly** — main **deliberative** body; the **'parliament of nations'**.
• **All members**; meets **once a year**; **one member, one vote**.
• Decisions by **majority**; important issues (peace, security) need **two-thirds majority**.
• Elects non-permanent SC members, ECOSOC members and (on SC recommendation) the Secretary-General; approves the budget.

**Security Council** — the **most important** organ; maintains **peace and security**.
• Only organ whose decisions are **binding** on members.
• **15 members:** **5 permanent — USA, UK, France, Russia, China**; **10 non-permanent** elected by the GA for **2 years**.
• **Veto:** a 'no' vote by any permanent member **cancels** a resolution → all five must agree.

| Organ | Key facts |
|---|---|
| **International Court of Justice** | Main **judicial** organ; **15 judges**, **9-year** term, no two from the same country; HQ **The Hague (Netherlands)** |
| **ECOSOC** | Economic and social cooperation; **54 members**, **3-year** term, elected by the GA |
| **Secretariat** | Day-to-day work; headed by the **Secretary-General** (**5-year** term, elected by the GA); organises conferences, drafts reports, prepares budget estimates |
| **Trusteeship Council** | Supervised **Trust Territories** (placed under **7** member states); all became independent by **1994** → work complete |

**Six principal organs:** GA · SC · ICJ · ECOSOC · Secretariat · Trusteeship Council.

**Functions**
• **Peacekeeping forces** (personnel from member states) sent to areas after conflict.
• Protects **human rights**.
• Technical help — **judicial structures, drafting constitutions**.
• **Humanitarian aid** — food, water, shelter for people displaced by war, famine, disasters.
• Development through **UNDP**.

**Achievements**
• Not always able to prevent war, but has **restored peace** effectively.
• **Sanctions on South Africa** helped end **apartheid**.
• Success in **health, child welfare, labour, education**.
• Efforts to end the **nuclear arms race** and promote peaceful nuclear energy.
• Needed more than ever against **terrorism and communal hatred**.

fiveW.who: UNESCO, UNICEF, WHO, ILO and others
fiveW.when: ILO 1919; UNESCO and UNICEF 1946; WHO 7 April 1948; UNDP 1965
fiveW.where: Paris (UNESCO), Geneva (WHO, ILO), New York (UNICEF, UNDP)
fiveW.what: Bodies that work for education, children, health, workers
fiveW.why: Peace also needs an end to poverty, hunger, disease and illiteracy
fiveW.how: Programmes, research, campaigns, aid and awareness

notes.content:
| Agency | Founded | HQ | Work |
|---|---|---|---|
| **UNESCO** | Nov **1946** | **Paris** | Peace through **education, science, culture**; research in developing countries; **preserves cultural heritage** |
| **UNICEF** | **1946** | New York | Originally *International Children's Emergency Fund* — food, clothes, healthcare for children after WWII; child health, education, fights **child labour**; first greeting card **1949** |
| **WHO** | **7 April 1948** (**World Health Day**) | **Geneva** | **'Health for all'**; campaigns against AIDS, cholera, malaria, COVID-19 |
| **ILO** | **1919** — **first specialised agency** | **Geneva** | Rights at work, **social justice for workers**, social security |
| **UNDP** | **1965** | New York | Development help |

**Other agencies:** **World Bank** (loans to developing countries) · **IMF** (monetary cooperation) · **ICAO** (air transport safety) · **ITU** (telecommunication) · **WMO** (weather and climate research) · **WTO** (international trade).

questions.question: Why was the UN set up? Why did the League of Nations fail?
questions.answer:
• League: kept peace in its early years, but in the 1930s the Axis Powers (Germany, Italy, Japan) grew powerful and it could not stop them → World War II (1939).
  • UN: set up in 1945 to prevent another world war, maintain international peace and security, and promote cooperation, human rights and social progress.

questions.question: Trace the formation of the United Nations.
questions.answer:
• 14 Aug 1941: Atlantic Charter — Churchill and Roosevelt; its proposals became the basis of the UN.
  • Jan 1942: 26 countries signed the Declaration by United Nations.
  • 25 Apr 1945: San Francisco Conference — 50 nations drafted the UN Charter.
  • 24 Oct 1945: UN came into existence with 51 members — UN Day.
questions.topperTip: Four dates in order = four marks.

questions.question: State the objectives of the UN.
questions.answer:
• Maintain international peace and security.
  • Promote human rights and equal rights for all.
  • Save future generations from war.
  • Promote justice, freedom and social progress.
  • Respect international law and treaties.

questions.question: Describe the composition and functions of the General Assembly.
questions.answer:
• Composition: all 193 member states; each has one vote; meets once a year.
  • Functions: (i) discusses world problems — a 'parliament of nations'; (ii) decisions by majority, important ones (peace, security) by two-thirds majority; (iii) elects non-permanent SC members, ECOSOC members and the Secretary-General; approves the budget.

questions.question: What is veto power?
questions.answer: A special power of the five permanent members of the Security Council — USA, UK, France, Russia, China. A negative vote by any one of them cancels a resolution, so all five must agree on every decision.

questions.question: Why is the Security Council considered the most important UN organ?
questions.answer:
• It is responsible for maintaining international peace and security.
  • Other organs only make recommendations; the Security Council's decisions are binding on all members.
  • It has 15 members, with 5 permanent members holding veto power.

questions.question: How many judges are there in the ICJ? What is their term?
questions.answer: 15 judges, elected for a 9-year term; no two judges can be from the same country. The ICJ sits at The Hague, Netherlands.

questions.question: Why was the Trusteeship Council established?
questions.answer: To supervise the administration of Trust Territories — territories that were not fully independent and had been placed under seven member states. By 1994 all of them had become independent or self-governing.

questions.question: (Picture) Head of the UN Secretariat: what is the designation, who elects the holder and what does the office do?
questions.answer:
• Designation: Secretary-General of the United Nations (identify the name from the photo in your book).
  • Elected by the General Assembly (on the Security Council's recommendation) for 5 years.
  • Secretariat's work: organises conferences, drafts reports, prepares budget estimates and carries out tasks set by other UN bodies.

questions.question: 'The world needs organisations like the UN more than ever today.' Do you agree? What role does the UN play in world peace?
questions.answer:
Yes.

  • Peacekeeping forces prevent fighting from resuming after conflicts.
  • The Security Council takes binding decisions; sanctions ended apartheid.
  • Works against the nuclear arms race, protects human rights, gives humanitarian aid.
  • Threats like terrorism, communal hatred, pandemics and climate change need global cooperation.
  • Though it has not prevented every war, no world war has occurred since 1945.

questions.question: What is the mission of UNESCO? State the functions of UNICEF and WHO.
questions.answer:
• UNESCO (Paris, 1946): peace through education, science and culture — promotes education, funds research, preserves cultural heritage.
  • UNICEF (1946): child health, education, nutrition; helps run child care centres; fights child labour.
  • WHO (Geneva, 7 April 1948): 'health for all'; campaigns against AIDS, cholera, malaria, COVID-19; promotes research.
